title: Pauli-resolved virtual distillation
authors: Si-Yuan Chen, Congcong Zheng, Kun Wang, Ming-Cheng Chen
abstract: Learning the full Pauli profile of the virtually distilled quantum state $ρ^m/\text{tr}(ρ^m)$ has so far required exponentially many copies of $ρ$. We show that all $4^n$ squared Pauli moments $[\text{tr}(Pρ^m)]^2$ can be learned to additive error $\varepsilon$ with confidence $1-δ$ from one $2m$-replica measurement setting using $O(m[n+\log(1/δ)]/\varepsilon^2)$ copies. This is an exponential speedup in the system size $n$ over previous protocols. For $m = 2$, we propose the coherent Bell difference sampling circuit that realizes this measurement on current devices. The speedup originates from paired replicas that cancel the anticommutation signs of Pauli operators, collapsing the incompatibility of the Pauli family. We certify this collapse by introducing the quantum Bernstein norm, a computable incompatibility measure for nonlinear functionals. A further information-theoretic $m$-replica protocol recovers the signed moments $\text{tr}(Pρ^m)$ using $O(m[n+\log(1/δ)]/\varepsilon^4)$ copies. For fixed $m$ in the stated lower-bound regime, it attains the optimal replica number, since any protocol with fewer replicas requires exponentially many copies.
summary: This paper presents a breakthrough in quantum state tomography by developing the quantum Bernstein norm to quantify joint measurement limitations. It demonstrates an exponential speedup in estimating the full Pauli profile of a quantum state by utilizing paired replica measurements. This significantly improves the resource scaling required for characterizing complex quantum states.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of learning the full Pauli profile of a virtually distilled quantum state, which previously required an exponentially large number of quantum state copies.
main_result: They achieve an exponential speedup by showing that the family of squared Pauli moments can be jointly measured using only $O(m[n + \log(1/\delta)]/\epsilon^2)$ copies, and a further protocol estimates signed moments with $O(m[n + \log(1/\delta)]/\epsilon^4)$ copies.
method: The core method involves developing the quantum Bernstein norm, a computable incompatibility measure, and utilizing paired replica measurements to cancel anticommutation signs, enabling joint estimation of many observables simultaneously.
model_or_system: The focus is on quantum states $ho$ and their $m$-replica versions $ho_m$ in an $n$-qubit system. The analysis is highly abstract, dealing with Pauli operators $\mathcal{P}_n$ and the estimation of their moments.
key_observables: The primary observables are the squared Pauli moments $\{ [	ext{tr}(Pho_m)]^2 \}_{P \in \mathcal{P}_n}$ and the signed Pauli moments $	ext{tr}(Pho_m)$.
important_parameters: System size $n$, replica number $m$, additive error $\epsilon$, and confidence parameter $\delta$.
main_assumptions: The joint measurability is achieved by constructing commuting operators on $2m$ replicas, and the analysis relies on the computability of the quantum Bernstein norm via SDPs.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the Coherent Bell Difference Sampling (CBDS) circuit for $m=2$, showing how four replicas are used for measurement. Figure 2 illustrates the operational meaning of the quantum Bernstein norm using a $k$-copy POVM.
paper_structure: The paper develops the quantum Bernstein norm as a measure of joint estimation capability, applies it to show the joint measurability of squared Pauli moments in a single $2m$-replica setting, and then presents a separate protocol to recover the signed moments.
why_interesting: This work provides significant theoretical advancements in quantum tomography and resource estimation, showing how structural properties (like paired replicas) can overcome exponential scaling barriers in quantum measurement protocols.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. The coherent Bell difference sampling (CBDS) circuit. Four replicas of ρ enter two Bell measurement blocks, acting on replicas (1, 2) and (3, 4). Transversal CNOT layers coherently subtract the Bell sampling outcomes of replicas (1, 2) from replicas (3, 4) before any readout. Measuring replicas (3, 4) yields Bell difference outcomes di that select a Pauli sector; conditioned on di, each site of replicas (1, 2) is read either in the computational basis (blue) or within a collective GHZ-type projector (red), returning the eigenvalue of OP in that sector (SM [24], Appendix A). A single run updates the estimators of all 4n squared moments [tr(Pρ2)]2 simultaneously.

FIG. 2. Operational meaning of the k-replica quantum Bern- stein norm ∥F∥k. A common k-copy POVM on ρ⊗k pro- duces a classical outcome j. The post-processing function hα(j) forms an unbiased estimator for each target functional fα. The ∥F∥k is the minimum possible range of these post- processing functions. Thus, a small ∥F∥k means that the nonlinear properties in F can be jointly estimated without bias and with small overhead.
